about.title: Mountain View Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Work in Mountain View looks different from block to block. Some people spend the day in office parks along Shoreline Boulevard; others deliver, build, cook, clean, or drive for a living across Santa Clara County. Getting hurt on the clock can happen in any of those settings, and the path forward is not always obvious. Workers' compensation usually covers medical care and part of your lost wages no matter who was at fault, and it is normally the only claim you can bring against your employer. But when someone outside your company caused the harm — a subcontractor on a job site, a property owner who ignored a hazard, a manufacturer of faulty equipment, or another driver — a separate injury claim may be possible. That last category matters here: Mountain View recorded 422 injury collisions in 2025 with 565 people hurt, and anyone whose job puts them on US-101 or El Camino Real is part of that traffic. LawProactive is a free service that connects you with an independent attorney who can sort out which claims fit your situation.

items.question: I was hit on US-101 while making a delivery for my Mountain View employer. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It may be both. Because you were working, your medical care and part of your lost wages would normally go through workers' compensation, regardless of who caused the crash. If another driver was at fault, you may also have a separate injury claim against that driver, which follows California's two-year deadline. An attorney can help you pursue both without one undercutting the other.

items.question: Can I sue my employer if the injury was clearly their fault?
items.answer: In most cases, no. California makes workers' compensation the exclusive remedy against your employer, even when the employer was careless. The exception is a negligent third party — a subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or another driver — who can be held responsible in a separate claim. Sorting out who counts as a third party is often the key question.

items.question: I'm worried about being fired for reporting my injury. What should I do?
items.answer: Report it anyway, and do so within 30 days, because that window matters for your workers' compensation claim. California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report an injury or file a claim. If you believe you are being punished for it, tell the attorney you are connected with, since that can become part of your case.
